extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (U.S. patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and limits governing amendment (re-issue) of U.S. letters patent — what defects a re-issue may correct, what changes are forbidden, and how to determine whether a re-issue is for the same invention as originally attempted to be described and claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of re-issue (defects of statement only)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The sole office of a re-issue is to correct faults of statement in the description and claim of the original patent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-issue is a remedy for mistakes in specification drafting (to relieve inventor from lack of skill in drawing specification and to prevent the public from taking undue advantage). It is intended to make the patent 'better' by correcting statement defects, allowing repeated re-issues until language corresponds exactly with the actual invention intended to be protected. It is not intended to remedy mistakes in an inventor's choice or judgment as to what to attempt to cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: No new matter may be introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: "No new matter shall be introduced into the specification."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prohibition is general and forbids adding substantive matter that would change the invention or introduce subject-matter proper to a separate application. Amendments adding 'new substantive matter' (i.e., matter that would have been the subject of another application) are impermissible. The 1870 Act and Revised Statutes repeat this bar. Cases cited repeatedly invalidate re-issues that introduce new inventions or material not originally presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue must be for the same invention as the original patent
rubrics_metrics.description: "A re-issue must be for the same invention as the original patent, and cannot be expanded to cover intervening inventions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A re-issue cannot lawfully embrace subject-matter the patentee did not endeavor to describe and claim in the original specification. Courts will construe re-issue claims narrowly; where a re-issued patent 'will bear no construction which confines its subject-matter to this invention,' its claims are invalid. The inventor seeking to capture a distinct or broader invention must file a new application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot introduce a different principle or other forms not within original limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "The re-issue cannot introduce a different principle though it were known to the patentee when he obtained the original patent" and "where the original patent accurately defines the invention, a re-issue cannot embrace antecedent improvements not within the limits of the original patent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the patentee knew other principles or forms at the time of the original patent, the re-issue may not be used to claim a different underlying principle or other forms of the invention beyond the original's defined limits. Where original patent covers but one form of an invention, re-issue cannot be used to cover other forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot claim matter discovered by using the original invention or later inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: "Matter discovered by using the original invention cannot be embraced in the re-issue" and "a re-issue cannot embrace later inventions, no matter how meritorious."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property of matter or new discoveries made after the original patent date cannot be appropriated via re-issue. If usefulness depends on properties of matter discovered after issuance, re-issue cannot claim and appropriate that property. Later-developed inventions must be pursued by new and independent applications; attempting to absorb them in a re-issue is forbidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot correct errors of judgment as to what to claim
rubrics_metrics.description: "An error in judgment as to what the patent shall cover, or in conclusions of fact, is no ground for a re-issue" and "an error in judgment as to the nature of the invention cannot be corrected by re-issue."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes that are matters of selection, strategy, or substantive judgment about claim scope are not remediable by re-issue. Courts distinguish inadvertent omission from deliberate choice or mistaken judgment; the latter cannot be fixed by re-issuing the same patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue available for inadvertence, accident, or mistake in statement
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue is permissible to correct inadvertence, accident, or mistake in the original specification so as to protect "just what he invented" — i.e., to state clearly and accurately what the inventor actually made and intended to claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain re-issue on this basis, the patentee must show that he honestly attempted to describe and claim the invention in the original application but failed through inadvertence, accident, or mistake. Re-issue thus can remedy defects of statement so that the patent describes the invention the inventor actually made and attempted to protect. Courts will require good faith and evidence of the original attempt; cases emphasize jealousy against any attempt to enlarge scope beyond the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step conception/practice test for what belongs to original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatise sets out four steps an inventor must have taken to be entitled to patent subject-matter: (1) conceive an idea of means and reduce it to practice; (2) perceive essential character with sufficient completeness for reproduction; (3) determine to patent entire invention or separable parts and apply; (4) incorporate in the application a specification that attempts to describe/claim that which he intends to secure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only subject-matter that the inventor had actually invented, comprehended, selected as the subject-matter of his patent, and attempted to describe and claim in the original specification (even if imperfectly) can be embraced by re-issue. Possibilities or undeveloped aspects perceived but not reduced to practice or claimed do not form part of the original invention for re-issue purposes; later developments require new patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for whether suggested/indicated matters in drawings/models/specification are part of original invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters 'suggested or indicated' in the original specification, drawings, or Patent Office model are not automatically part of the invention intended to be covered; they may be included in re-issue only if a comparison of the two patents shows the original intended to embrace them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will compare the original and re-issued patents: only if the original patent (specification, drawings, or model) fairly embraced the things now claimed will the re-issue be deemed to cover them. Merely being suggested or indicated is insufficient unless it is apparent that the original intended to secure them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue cannot appropriate inventions for which original patent rights have expired or are limited by foreign patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issue cannot claim matter for which the original has expired or which is limited in effect by foreign patents; to cover matters excluded by such limitations would be impermissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parts of the invention were covered by expired foreign patents or excluded by the reasons for limitation, the re-issue cannot revive or appropriate them. Similarly, one cannot expand a claim by re-issue so as to cover subject-matter the original patent no longer had rights to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope determination is by construction against enlargement; courts presume Patent Office acted properly
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine the limits of the invention originally attempted, the Patent Office and courts must construe the original patent; courts are logically and legally compelled to presume the Patent Office performed its duty, and courts will regard attempts to enlarge scope by re-issue with 'jealousy and disfavor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When scope is ambiguous, the courts construe re-issue narrowly and assume the original application defined the invention intended to be secured. Decisions emphasize that re-issue should be confined to curing defects of description/claims and not used to appropriate other inventors' subsequent achievements; any claimed enlargement will be scrutinized and likely invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue may correct term/clerical errors and make claims conformable to rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-issue may correct clerical or statement errors (e.g., fixing the term of a patent so as to conform to a foreign patent previously granted) and may modify claims to make them more conformable to the patentee's exact rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts recognize narrow corrective uses of re-issue such as clarifying specification, correcting term errors, or altering claim form to conform to what the patentee actually invented, provided no new matter or broader invention is introduced. Examples include re-stating a patent to include what was plainly the subject but not fully secured due to misstatement of principles.
